articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council approved the issuance of Requests for Proposals (RFP) for underwriting services of general obligation bonds for the Piedmont Community Pool at its August 16 meeting. The scope of services that will be provided by the selected investment bank will be in the full range of investment banking, marketing, and underwriting services required in connection with the authorization of the general obligation bonds in the amount of $19.5 million. The underwriter will remain in place until the issuance of bonds is completed. “The City of Piedmont has not been to the [bond underwriting] markets before. We expect the city to get a very high credit rating, but we want someone who will be able to explain...what makes Piedmont great,” City Finance Director Michael Szczech told city council. “We can do that through a negotiated sale, and we can educate the underwriter who then goes out and markets the bond to investors, who can reflect all the things that make Piedmont, Piedmont.” He added that a competitive sale, rather than a negotiated sale approach, does not have that opportunity for education. “We can instruct the underwriter to place ads in local papers, just to make sure that residents know this is available, and that they have every opportunity to purchase them,” Szczech explained. The city will seek proposals from investments banks to serve as the sole underwriter for its proposed issuance of general obligation bonds. The bonds will bear a fixed rate of interest to maturity, with a final maturity of 30 years. articles.text: A draft of the Piedmont Safer Streets (PSS) plan, an update of the 2014 Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan, is now available for public review. The PSS plan includes chapters on the context and need for the plan, the community needs assessment, recommended projects, and prioritization and implementation. The draft plan is the result of a thorough public engagement effort. The first step was conducting a community needs assessment from mid-November 2020 through early January 2021, during which the City received over 2,500 individual comments. The next step in the process was to generate recommendations based on the community needs assessment while also addressing the City’s ongoing concerns. At the April 22, 2021 Pedestrian Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC) virtual meeting, project consultant Niko Letunic presented a draft set of recommended projects to be included in the PSS plan. The Photo by Paul Kuroda The city seeks input from the community on its draft of the Piedmont Safer Streets (PSS) plan. PBAC received public comments on the draft recommendations, discussed the matter and recommended revisions that resulted in the draft PSS plan currently posted for public review. In addition to the list of recommended projects to improve pedestrian and bicycle safety, the PSS plan includes a chapter on prioritization and implementation that focuses on quickbuild projects, bike corridors, and lays out a priority list for the recommended “enhanced street crossings.” The quick build projects section includes several traffic calming measures such as speed humps, speed tables, build-outs, chicanes and mini-round about.
articles.title: City seeks public input on Safer Streets Plan

Is it possible the author believes she can telepathically channel black people without ever having to meet any of them? Gallup polls suggest that 81 percent of those polled want more policing nationwide. Oakland Police Chief LeRonne Armstrong lamented that a 90 percent homicide spike occurred following $150 million cuts as black murder victim rates skyrocketed in police-defunded cities. But truly supporting black lives means taking unpopular positions at the risk of offending [people] on NextDoor. Abolitionism wasn’t the chic fad that wokeness is.

articles.text: As reported in Piedmont Post’s article “Piedmont an Outlier...” (7/28/2021), the Piedmont City Council voted unanimously not to appeal the city’s state-mandated Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) goal of 587 new housing units, as part of the city’s updated 2023-2031 Housing Element. We are proud of this decision. It indicates our city’s willingness to take a solutions-oriented role in tackling the dire Bay Area housing shortage. A recent article in the San Francisco Chronicle, “Bay Area Cities Face Long Odds in Fighting State-Mandated Housing Goals,” (7/23/2021) suggests that most of the 28 cities which challenged their RHNA quotas did so because their elected leaders were posturing to constituents resistant to local growth. Piedmont’s city staff and attorney pointed out a RHNA appeal would have been a waste of time and money: In Southern California, where the RHNA cycle is ahead of northern California, more than 50 cities appealed their allocations and only two received minor adjustments down. The RHNA allocations are significantly higher during the upcoming cycle because we are in a housing crisis and need a lot more housing. Cities like Piedmont are being asked to do their fair share. Instead of considering the allocations a burden, we should support our local leaders for being advocates of housing equity and inclusion. These 587 units will not be added overnight. The state does not require cities to build the units, only to take the first steps by removing obstacles that currently stand in the way, such as single-family zoning, which is how almost all Piedmont is currently zoned. articles.text: KQED, Northern California’s National Public Radio (NPR) station, has announced an allday block party on September 25 to celebrate its newly-designed headquarters on Mariposa The newly renovated-headquarters transforms the office building from industrial-style to an accessible, state-of-theart center. It was designed by the award-winning San Francisco-based architecture firm The station purchased the building in 1991, when KQED’s primary focus was television and radio production. Presently, KQED serves audiences on broadcast as well as through digital media tools like social media and web, podcasts, and live and virtual events. Since 1991, the station’s staff has doubled and its content services have expanded. It is now home to one of the largest newsrooms “KQED will redefine public media for the Bay Area, making it more diverse, participatory and community powered,” said Michael Isip, KQED President and CEO. “The new headquarters will enable our staff to thrive in providing crucial programming and education services and will expand possibilities for our community to come together to find common ground.” The new design features modernized production and studio spaces, expanding KQED’s ability to provide quality digital programming. EHDD’s design also increases visibility to the public; a new corner entry at Mariposa and Bryant Streets establishes a more prominent position in the Mission Street neighborhood with a glass facade. “We’re lifting up the façade to invite the community in,” said Rebecca Sharkey, EHDD Principal. “This new building represents the physical place of KQED engagement, a place to connect face-to-face with journalists and neighbors, to experience the breadth of KQED content, and to engage in dialogue about issues that matter most to the Bay Area and beyond.” KQED Grand Opening KQED will host a free, allday open house and block party on Saturday, September 25, unveiling its newly designed headquarters to the public. The community is invited to participate in an array of live programs and performances, featuring notable guests and radio personalities from KQED, NPR, Public Broadcasting Station (PBS) and PBS kids. There will also be workshops, media-making activities, and family and kid-friendly games throughout the building. “In a protracted time of separation and isolation, we’ve learned how to better use digital tools for virtual dialogue and participation.” Isip said. “We’ll continue to use technology to fill gaps and extend the reach of our work. Bringing people together for personal connection is essential for a strong, vibrant community.” For more information about the block party and open house, visit kqed.org/events.

articles.text: Piedmont Police Officer Hugo Diaz was named the Juvenile Liaison Officer for Piedmont School District in May. Piedmont Police Officer Hugo Diaz was named the new Juvenile Liaison Officer for Piedmont School District, in May this year. His role is designed to provide a stable connection between students and the police. Diaz, 33, is a former teacher and artist who grew up in East Oakland and attended Castlemont High School. He earned a B.A. in Art at Cal State East Bay and then earned a Master’s in Graphic Design. But at age 30, he decided to pursue a career in law enforcement and began working with the campus police department at Cal State. It was thre that he saw a flier advertising police work in Piedmont. At the time he did not know much about Piedmont. After doing a bit of research, he became interested in the possibility of working in a small city with a focus on its children. He was hired in June 2019. His position as Juvenile Liaison Officer is funded through a grant from the state by the tobacco industry. “The schools are still in charge of discipline. I’m more of a resource to the schools; I’m there so students can familiarize themselves with me and vice versa. This position serves to minimize police activity at the school,” he said. The Piedmont Police Department has had juvenile officers primarily for middle and high school students for many years. In his short time in the role, Diaz has interviewed students, spoken on podcasts, and has communicated with principals to learn what they expect of him. Diaz has received training on issues of sexual assault, dating violence, active shooter response, drug and alcohol abuse, crisis intervention, mental illness, and title IX issues. He will work Tuesday to Friday during school hours while on regular police patrol work. He will be responsible for responding to any needs at the schools. He can be contacted at the police department at 510-420-3056 (hdiaz@piedmont.ca.gov).

articles.text: Residents invited to display classic cars on Sept. 6 The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 3rd annual Car Show on Labor Day morning, Monday, September 6. The cars will be displayed in the parking lot in front of the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. In 2019, the last time the event took place, a total of 44 gleaming vehicles were on display. Peet’s Coffee will be served, and neighbors are invited to meet members of the police department while viewing and chatting with the car owners. In 2018 the Piedmont Police Department decided to rev up the event by adding classic cars to the mix. The community responded enthusiastically, and more than 1600 people showed up. “I value the Piedmont Police Department Car Show because I believe it builds strong relationships between community members and their police department,” said Officer Tyler Petit, who has coordinated the show since 2018. “The mutual trust between our police department and the community we serve is essential in maintaining public safety and effective policing. I’ll do whatever it takes to maintain that public trust.” Piedmont residents interested in participating in the city’s own Concours d’Elegance are asked to contact Officer Petit at tpetit@ piedmont.ca.gov. Include your name, address, email, and phone number along with the year, make and model of your car. articles.text: On August 11, Tomás J. Aragón, MD, DrPH, Director and State Public Health Officer, issued an order on Vaccine Verification for Workers in Schools. In reading the directive one discovers that it does not mandate that school staff be vaccinated, but does provide a requirement for testing all adults unless proof of vaccination has been submitted to the school. It clarifies that only a vaccination may support an exemption from testing. “Previous history of COVID-19 from which the individual recovered more than 90 days earlier, or a previous positive antibody test for COVID-19, do not waive this requirement for testing,” the order states. Before discovering the numbers of faculty and staff who do not exercise the option of submitting proof of vaccination, it is difficult to accurately predict the cost in dollars and logistical support that will be required to fulfill Piedmont School District’s obligations under this new order. It would appear the amount will be substantive. This can be said without factoring in how small the number of individuals being tested may be. Even assuming the per-test cost to be linear, the fixed costs of implementation, documentation and ongoing monitoring lifts the y axis intercept well above zero. However, there may be an even greater consequence to consider than what comes with abiding by the delineated parameters of the order. That heightened impact lives in the question, “How do we work together?” PUSD and our community demonstrated a capacity to navigate the rise of the Delta variant, and reopened schools in a manner commonly described as very positive. The community’s mutual success in this accomplishment, in the quest to foster thriving students, is nothing short of heroic. Individuals subjugated their own worst fears around the safety (be it physical health or mental health) of primarily our students, but also ourselves and one another. Our first week of school has ended; some fears have not. To offer some transparency, I am sharing here words that I earlier sent out to APT [Association of Piedmont Teachers] members as we prepared for our first day of the school year. “I am most of all very optimistic about our return to school, moderately concerned about physical safety of students and staff, and gravely concerned about the potential for deep and long-lasting harm to our community relationships if we begin to argue unproductively. I feel confident by the response I have received from board members and district administration that they share these concerns and have a heightened interest in including our perspectives in an unprecedented way moving forward.” I can now add that the district has continued to build on that interest, not only with APT, but with all PUSD community members. Challenging times do not automatically bring out the best in people. They can, but the same boiling water that softens the potato hardens the egg. Another thought initially shared with my APT peers is extended to our entire community now. “Let us work together and not divide. We can disagree and we can be passionate, and yet we can also still be colleagues and mutually respectful. We are modeling for our students how to navigate difficult times with differences of opinion. Let us model well for them!” Flint Christensen, a Computer Science teacher at Piedmont High School, is President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT).
articles.title: Vaccination and Testing to impact PUSD

articles.text: Results of the White Bread Challenge How important is it to wash your hands? As kids go back to school, it is more important than ever for them to be practicing good hygiene habits. This means washing your hands, covering your cough, etc. This hands-on experiment demonstrates the importance of thoroughly washing your hands through powerful visualizations and observations. Learn how clean…and dirty household and classroom items are using the white bread experiment. Suggested Materials: • Enough slices of fresh, white bread for each item you’d like to test • 1 plastic sealable sandwich bag for each slice of bread that you’ll test • A slice of bread that has not been touched (use gloves or clean tongs) • Predictions, Observations, and Data Worksheet • Whatever items are frequently touched in your home or classroom: • Clean hands: warm water and soap for 20 seconds • Clean hands: hand sanitizer • Dirty hands • Your face • Anything with a touch screen • Phone • Keyboard • TV remote or gaming controller • Door handle • Light switch • Favorite book • Favorite toy • Your pillow Procedure: 1. Using new gloves or clean tongs, remove 1 slice of fresh white bread and seal it in a plastic sandwich bag. a. Number and label the bag as Control bag #1, etc. 2. Wipe dry, clean hands that have been washed thoroughly for at least 20 seconds with soap and warm water on the next slice of bread. Photo by Jaralee Annice Metcalf a. Number and label the bag as Clean hands- Soap and Warm Water (bag #2) 3. Continue to repeat this process for each surface you’d like to test. Make sure to correctly label and number each bag. 4. Leave the sealed bags with their labels on a table or counter for up to one month. 5. Make predictions about which slices of bread will grow the most mold. Which slices will get moldy the fastest? pages.text: Wednesday, August 18, 2021 7 Vaccination and Testing to impact PUSD By Flint Christensen On August 11, Tomás J. Aragón, MD, DrPH, Director and State Public Health Officer, issued an order on Vaccine Verification for Workers in Schools. In reading the directive one discovers that it does not mandate that school staff be vaccinated, but does provide a requirement for testing all adults unless proof of vaccination has been submitted to the school. It clarifies that only a vaccination may support an exemption from testing. “Previous history of COVID-19 from which the individual recovered more than 90 days earlier, or a previous positive antibody test for COVID-19, do not waive this requirement for testing,” the order states. Before discovering the numbers of faculty and staff who do not exercise the option of submitting proof of vaccination, it is difficult to accurately predict the cost in dollars and logistical support that will be required to fulfill Piedmont School District’s obligations under this new order. It would appear the amount will be substantive. This can be said without factoring in how small the number of individuals being tested may be. Even assuming the per-test cost to be linear, the fixed costs of implementation, documentation and ongoing monitoring lifts the y axis intercept well above zero. However, there may be an even greater consequence to consider than what comes with abiding by the delineated parameters of the order. That heightened impact lives in the question, “How do we work together?” PUSD and our community demonstrated a capacity to navigate the rise of the Delta variant, and reopened schools in a manner commonly described as very positive. The community’s mutual success in this accomplishment, in the quest to foster thriving students, is nothing short of heroic. Individuals subjugated their own worst fears around the safety (be it physical health or mental health) of primarily our students, but also ourselves and one another. Our first week of school has ended; some fears have not. To offer some transparency, I am sharing here words that I earlier sent out to APT [Association of Piedmont Teachers] members as we prepared for our first day of the school year. “I am most of all very optimistic about our return to school, moderately concerned about physical safety of students and staff, and gravely concerned about the potential for deep and long-lasting harm to our community relationships if we begin to argue unproductively. I feel confident by the response I have received from board members and district administration that they share these concerns and have a heightened interest in including our perspectives in an unprecedented way moving forward.” I can now add that the district has continued to build on that interest, not only with APT, but with all PUSD community members. Challenging times do not automatically bring out the best in people. They can, but the same boiling water that softens the potato hardens the egg. Another thought initially shared with my APT peers is extended to our entire community now. “Let us work together and not divide. We can disagree and we can be passionate, and yet we can also still be colleagues and mutually respectful. We are modeling for our students how to navigate difficult times with differences of opinion. Let us model well for them!” Flint Christensen, a Computer Science teacher at Piedmont High School, is President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT). articles.text: On January 15 two years ago, Atticus Lim, then a sophomore at Piedmont High School, made a routine defensive move in a basketball game. It would change the trajectory of his life. Lim slid his feet left to stay in front of the opposing player with the ball. It caused his opponent to lose the ball. In the process, Lim fell backwards and his head hit the court, hard. It’s a fairly routine play in basketball and no whistle was blown to stop the play. The clock kept ticking. But Lim’s personal life took a time out. He was diagnosed with having suffered a severe traumatic brain injury. Atticus wasn’t able to return to school for six weeks, and even then, he struggled to keep up with his studies. And then in March 2020 the coronavirus pandemic arrived, and classes began to be taught on computers. Persistent online class meant an increase in screen time – the worst possible learning environment for someone recovering from a traumatic brain injury. He began experiencing the worst headaches of his life. Recovery from a traumatic brain injury can take two years or more, and Lim hasn’t fully recovPiedmont High School senior Atticus Lim shoots three-point baskets with friend Charlie Olcott in a fundraising effort to help individuals with traumatic brain injuries. ered. His brain injury was in the worst 2-5 percent. “[The doctor] told Atticus that the best thing he could do [when recovering] was to exercise,” explained Atticus’ father, Dion Lim. “You can think of it like spraining your brain - you certainly want to rest it, but you also want to get circulation in there.” Fast forward to the recent start of the 2021 school year. Atticus is back in school and doing better, but the recovery time from that one small moment in time is still ongoing. A relatively innocuous play on a basketball court has required two years of rewinding, reworking, patience and therapy. If you know the Lim family Atticus Lim floats up a shot in a 2018 basketball game versus Campolinda. you won’t be surprised to hear that Atticus has turned this negative experience into an opportunity to help others. Atticus joined a fundraising charity called SameYou, which was founded by the British actress Emilia Clarke (famous for her role in Game of Thrones). SameYou aims to develop better recovery treatment for survivors of brain injury and stroke. For his fundraiser, Atticus wanted to recover the joy of basketball, so he decided to shoot 33 three-pointers every day in July. He chose 33 to bring attention to the fact that one in three people will have an acquired brain injury at some point in their lives. Atticus has raised £4,500 of his goal of £5,000 (almost $7,000) to support those with traumatic brain injuries. “I reached out to basically everyone I know, trying to gain support, donations or a pledge for each basket made,” Lim said. “I got my friends to rebound my shots for me, to support the message of rebounding from an injury.” An estimated 2,500,000 high school students report having a traumatic brain injury every year. articles.text: Countless words have been written about the impact of the pandemic – the effects of familial loss, social distancing, mask wearing, isolation and resultant loneliness. I recently came across an article in the New York Times written by social psychologist Jonathan Haidt and psychologist Jean M. Twenge whose research has linked loneliness at school to the ubiquitous use of the smartphone. It’s a theory that at first blush seems counterintuitive – aren’t kids perpetually engaging with one another on their devices? However, as in-person school is finally underway, their supposition is worth perusing. First, since 2012 the smartphone has been used by a majority of Americans, and by 2015 twothirds of all tweens/teens. Facebook, Instagram, TikTok etc. are social media platforms relied on for contact and interaction. But they also have become sources of anger (beginning with the “like button”) and criticism. Experts have posed the question as to whether smartphones and social media are actually harming teens. Of coursem there has been pushback, which has pointed out that a similar hyperbolic reaction occurred to kids reading comic books, listening to rock ‘n roll, watching television and playing video games. What Haidt and Twenge focused on in their research was the word “harm”, citing a study of international students conducted every three years since 2000, titled The Program for International Student Assessment (PISA). It has surveyed 15-yearolds in dozens of countries, and included questions about loneliness at school. The psychologists, expanding the definition of “harm”, state that loneliness is not the same as depression, but the two are often correlated, meaning lonely teens are often depressed teens and visa versa. In a paper, recently published by the psychologists in the Journal of Adolescence, they found that in 36 out of 37 countries loneliness at school has accelerated dramatically since 2012, which coincides with the embrace of the smartphone by teens. The data shows that this phenomenon has doubled in the last nine years in Europe, Latin America, America, and English-speaking countries. In other words, the two researchers conclude that the smartphone has brought about a “planetary rewiring of human communication that has transformed peer and family relationships as well as the texture of daily life for everyone.” They go on to say that it is harder to stoke up a casual conversation when everyone is staring down at their phones, or have a deep conversation when each party is interrupted by buzzing or vibrating notifications. Their data also indicates that teen mental health has changed for the worse since 2012. They argue that electronic communications are akin to empty calories, a kind of intermittent sugar rush, brief, but not comprising social interactions that are necessary for teens to become fully competent adults. Haidt and Twenge ask: what can we do to assure that our youngsters get the critical social intercourse so vital to their mental wellbeing? One offered solution is to prohibit the use of electronic devices at schools. On the way to school and on the way home, fine, but not during the school day. That would require adolescents to fully focus on those around them. I would add that learning to read the nuanced facial expressions and body language of kids and adults are acquired skills, ones not encouraged by the smartphone, whether texting or screen time. Another suggestion by the psychologists is to make it impossible for tweens and newbie teens to establish social media accounts. Even before the pandemic, teens were finding themselves increasingly lonely at school. And now, after the nearly 18 months of relative isolation, contagion fears, remote schooling, stressed parents, and increased reliance on their devices, the question begged is: will teens willingly put away their phones at school and learn to rely on in-person interactions? Haidt and Twenge say that we must help them do exactly that. Chris Honore’ resides in Ashland, Oregon and has been a columnist and reviewer in the Post for more than 20 years. articles.text: The summer days spent in Santa Barbara were slow and lazy. Our family spent five days in July exploring that quiet sea town, wading in the waves, lounging by the pool, and eating the best seafood I’ve ever tasted. The beachfront resort where we stayed had a Hawaiian feel to it projected by middle-aged men in cargo shorts, Tommy Bahamas shirts and Ray-ban glasses, to say nothing of the oversized pina coladas. Getting to Santa Barbara from Piedmont, on the other hand, was the opposite of relaxing. There’s Gilroy with its perennial traffic, lack of bathroom breaks, exploding chip bags, and constant disagreements with the GPS. My dad talks to it as if it were a real person. He challenges every left turn, right turn, and exit that is recommended. One time we nearly ran out of gas. It was 9 o’clock at night when we suddenly noticed the gas indicator was hovering around zero and the next gas station was 23 miles away. My mom drove in the mountains like it would be the final drive of her life if she didn’t make it to that gas station. And all those miles, according to the gas indicator, we were driving with an empty tank. Somehow, we made it. That adventure was nothing compared to our return trip. Remembering our difficulties with gas, we filled up our car before leaving the hidden paradise of Santa Barbara. It was agreed that my dad would be driving the first half of the way. I had put in my AirPods, started my playlist, and zoned out expecting a peaceful five-hour ride home. At some point I dozed off. When I awoke, my mom was at the wheel, which meant we had passed San Luis Obispo. I heard my parents debating whether to take the shortcut that Google maps was offering to avoid the traffic slowdown near Gilroy. {Sometimes I think the only reason Gilroy exists is to create slowdowns.} My dad wasn’t particularly excited by the shortcut offered by my mom’s GPS, and his phone wasn’t suggesting anything, but that could have been because he has such a bad relationship with his GPS. In the end, he too, didn’t want to be stalled in traffic near Gilroy, so my mom veered to the right and off 101. It was somewhat strange that what was advertised by Google as route 25 North looked like a twolane street. Once you go down the road there’s no way to go back unless you make a virtually impossible U-turn. The road itself was just hills, hills, and you guessed it, more hills. We were expecting to get back on 101, but Google had a surprise announcement: “Keep on 25 North for 55 miles.” As we climbed one mountain after another east of Gilroy, 101 was nowhere to be seen, let alone found. We had no choice but to trudge on. (To be fair I wasn’t surprised that something like this would happen; Google maps has been leading us astray since we started using it.) After driving on this lonely highway for lord knows how long, we came to a huge mound of dirt blocking the road. At this moment we thought this is it: this highway will be our final resting place. After a brief panic attack, we discovered a detour next to the original road. Once we got on it, it directed us back to Highway 25 and we continued our journey through rural California. After a good 20 miles or so, we passed a town sign for Paicines, with a population of less than 100. We discovered that it was an unincorporated town. It looked like a ghost town, with lizards and snakes as its only inhabitants. But oddly enough, despite seeing buildings falling apart and being in the middle of nowhere, there was a fully operational retro-looking gas station. There was actually color on the building, originally a vibrant light pink and green, now faded. Nonetheless it was still color, and seemed oddly out of place. After leaving Paicines, we passed what seemed to be a ravine or dry creek bed. Wrong. Our trusty friend Google revealed that we had just crossed the San Andreas Fault. Being a person who is deathly terrified of earthquakes, the revelation did not sit well with me at all. Imagine, if there was an earthquake, wouldn’t we be the ones that had the mountains crashing down on us, and no one would know what happened to us? And so we kept driving, through more ghost towns like Tres Pinos, with not a soul in sight. I thought that we would never get to the end of that road. It just went on for as far as my eye could see. pages.text: Wednesday, August 18, 2021 9 CRYSTAL’S REFLECTIONS By Crystal Vacker The summer days spent in Santa Barbara were slow and lazy. Our family spent five days in July exploring that quiet sea town, wading in the waves, lounging by the pool, and eating the best seafood I’ve ever tasted. The beachfront resort where we stayed had a Hawaiian feel to it projected by middle-aged men in cargo shorts, Tommy Bahamas shirts and Ray-ban glasses, to say nothing of the oversized pina coladas. Getting to Santa Barbara from Piedmont, on the other hand, was the opposite of relaxing. There’s Gilroy with its perennial traffic, lack of bathroom breaks, exploding chip bags, and constant disagreements with the GPS. My dad talks to it as if it were a real person. He challenges every left turn, right turn, and exit that is recommended. One time we nearly ran out of gas. It was 9 o’clock at night when we suddenly noticed the gas indicator was hovering around zero and the next gas station was 23 miles away. My mom drove in the mountains like it would be the final drive of her life if she didn’t make it to that gas station. And all those miles, according to the gas indicator, we were driving with an empty tank. Somehow, we made it. That adventure was nothing compared to our return trip. Remembering our difficulties with gas, we filled up our car before leaving the hidden paradise of Santa Barbara. It was agreed that my dad would be driving the first half of the way. I had put in my AirPods, started my playlist, and zoned out expecting a peaceful five-hour ride home. At some point I dozed off. When I awoke, my mom was at the wheel, which meant we had passed San Luis Obispo. In the end, he too, didn’t want to be stalled in traffic near Gilroy, so my mom veered to the right and off 101. It was somewhat strange that what was advertised by Google as route 25 North looked like a twolane street. We were expecting to get back on 101, but Google had a surprise announcement: “Keep on 25 North for 55 miles.” As we climbed one mountain after another east of Gilroy, 101 was nowhere to be seen, let alone found. We had no choice but to trudge on. (To be fair I wasn’t surprised that something like this would happen; Google maps has been leading us astray since we started using it.) articles.text: School is back in session, meaning the start of the 2021- 2022 sports schedule is right around the corner. articles.text: After 2021’s sports schedule jammed 9 months of sports into a three-month schedule, high schools throughout the country are welcoming back their new student-athletes. Piedmont’s athletes in the Class of 2022 looks to what could be a defining year of their high school careers. This week, the Post takes a look at two male and two female athletes in advance of the upcoming season: JoJo Murphy, Basketball What can we say about JoJo Murphy? The senior enters a critical year after leading last year’s 11-5 team in several categories; points at 409, knocking down 55 three-pointers with a sterling 43 shooting percentage, to go along with 105 rebounds, 58 assists, and 46 steals. He had five games when he scored 30 or more points, including a career-high of 38 against San Leandro on May 7. He also had seven 3-pointers against Bishop O’Dowd in the season-finale on June 4. He was named the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2020 after unseating former starter DaRon Benson for a first-team spot. He scored 385 points and helped lead Piedmont to its first North Coast Section championship. Murphy earned WestCoastPreps.com’s Bay Area Athlete of the Year award last month. And you can put him on the Piedmont Post’s Athlete of the Year watch list once again. Amanda Becker, Tennis & Soccer Amanda Becker, a starter at No. 1 doubles on Jim Landes’ tennis team last year, will be a team leader this fall. She Becker was dominant at the No. 1 spot, known for her aggressive play in front of the net; smashing volleys left, right, and center. She posted a 5-2 record in at doubles last season while teaming up with four different players – Audrey Mahaney, Mara LaForte, Kate Dorman, and Michaela Bini. She played on the soccer team as a freshman and sophomore and was an influential member of Dan Chubbock’s attack. She did not compete in soccer during the pandemic school year in 2020. Staff Photos JoJo Murphy recently won WestCoastPreps.com’s Bay Area Athlete of the Year award. He led Piedmont’s basketball team in nearly all categories last season. Amanda Becker is set for a big season on the tennis team this fall. Conner Curtis, Soccer Conner Curtis led the soccer team in scoring the past two seasons. He’s a versatile player, typically lining up in the Central Attacking Midfield role, but can rotate along the wing as well. As a team leader, he helped PHS finish with a 10-0-1 overall record with a perfect 10-0 record against Shoreline Division league teams. The team’s only loss came to non-league rival, Bishop O’Dowd, a 2-0 outcome. In 2021, Curtis scored at least eight goals and proved to be a free-kick specialist, taking every corner and set piece last season. He bagged a pair of goals against Alameda and scored on free-kick goals against Encinal and San Lorenzo. Curtis was named honorable mention for Sophomore of the Year in 2020 by the Post, and also honorable mention the prior year. Conner Curtis is the leading scorer on the soccer team. He’s a versatile player in coach Todd Sullivan’s system.

articles.text: Piedmont High Class of 2021 graduate Aidan Mitchell just finished up a summer that is unique by most standards. A former Swiss resident, he played baseball this summer with the Hünenberg Unicorns in the Swiss Baseball National League A. He has been competing in the Switzerland adult leagues since he was 15 years old. His teammates are college prospects around his age, ranging to veterans up in the 40s and 50s. “I was playing in the men’s league, and before I was in the Cadets, which is equivalent to around Middle School. You’d have some people in their 50s still playing, or some teenagers like me next to them. When I first got on the team, I was amazed that I was playing next to somebody in their mid-50s,” said Mitchell with a laugh. “There are usually former and current college players out there, it’s a good league. They bring people from all over and from a lot of different age groups. The rules aren’t different, but the makeup of teams is definitely something you won’t see in the U.S.,” he added. Mitchell and his family moved to Switzerland from Los Angeles seven years ago and lived there for five years before moving to Piedmont. He’s not the only Yankee there, though. Clubs often bring in ringers from the States. “One of the more interesting rules is that you can’t have a foreign-born player pitch in the first game, and they typically play two games a day. The good Swiss teams will pay to bring in players from the U.S.,” said Mitchell. Playing with men of different ages has allowed him the unique experience of pitching to his dad as catcher in a competitive game. “My favorite part of it was being able to play next to my dad. He played catcher in high school, so I was able to pitch to him. It was probably the most amazing experience to have him coach me, then get behind the dish and catch for me,” said Mitchell.

The Bay Area Panthers announced at a press conference on August 16 its plans to kick off its inaugural 2022 season in the Indoor Football League at San Jose’s SAP Center next March. Kurt Bryan, former Piedmont High football coach, will guide the team as head coach. articles.text: Paper books vs. iBooks for kids Given today’s widely popular digital reading devices and the rich tradition of children’s paper books, we are wondering which reading format is better suited for young readers’ learning. Do digital and paper books have the same effects on children’s story comprehension, or is one medium more beneficial? In reviewing the scientific literature addressing learning outcomes with digital and paper books for children at the earliest stages of reading development (early or emergent readers ages 1–8), we consider the traditional paper book scenario where early readers’ first experience of books is typically modeled and mediated by adults at home, vs. more current scenarios where early readers’ first experience of books may be e-books, picture book apps, story apps and iBooks accessed independently. Are we to expect a transition from print to digital that changes the established school and home routines of book reading? One element which emerges as significant is the quality of digital enhancements (voice and other digital features that make the story content accessible without adult interaction). Of the many types of digital enhancements used, content related enhancements which focus the children’s attention on and align with the storyline emerge as most beneficial. Alternatively, digital enhancements such as aesthetically based enhancements and embedded games may distract and decrease story comprehension. Another element which has been studied is the addition of on-line dictionaries embedded in digital texts. Do embedded digital dictionaries enhance story comprehension? Research shows that if the dictionary is dynamic (visual and audio), it can be beneficial for vocabulary development. However, the presence of the dictionary had no effect on story comprehension, suggesting that focusing attention on isolated word meanings may distract from the story content. Adult support effects have also been studied with regard to digital and paper books. At this point, studies demonstrate a clear advantage for adult mediated print book reading sessions, suggesting that (skilled) adults are better able to attune their support to children’s needs than enhanced digital books that the children read or listen to on their own. Instead of focusing on whether digital is better than paper, let’s consider the digital format to be a potential addition to paper which may open up new opportunities for book reading. For example, this technology could supplement absent or unskilled parents and teachers. Considering the low cost and accessibility of digital books, this could provide valuable supplementary reading material in homes where access is restricted. And, of course on-line reading has advantages, as we have all discovered during the pandemic, in situations where adults and children cannot read together in person. While the gold standard remains adult mediated print book reading sessions, to the extent that digital books have the potential to get more books into the hands of more kids, let’s do it. Kathryn Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing support. articles.text: Rodriguez The past 18 months have been challenging, to say the least: wildfires, drought, political unrest, social upheaval, and quarantine, not to mention a pandemic whose variants continue to leave the future uncertain. We all deserve a pat on the back for making it this far, albeit not unscathed. As adults, we can at least pretend to have some control over how we’ve navigated the pandemic. Our children, however, can’t really keep up that pretense. At a time in life when individuals can already feel powerless, our children have done more than their fair share of “rolling with the punches.” They’ve been unable to see family and friends. They’ve missed important coming-of-age moments like prom and graduation. They’ve had to learn how to navigate remote learning. And now, we ask them once more to adjust – they are returning to school full-time, in person. So, how do we best support our kids as they return to the new normal? First, it’s important to acknowledge that there may be some gaps, socially and academically. For many students, remote learning was challenging, and the structure and rigor of remote learning varied by school and subject. If your student seems to be dealing with some gaps in knowledge, don’t worry – they’re not alone and there are resources available to help. Many teachers hold office hours to address students’ questions. There are copious free or lowcost tutorials available online. If your student needs more individual attention, a peer or professional tutor may make the most sense. Helping your student develop good study habits is another important step in starting the school year strong and keeping the momentum going throughout the year. Students who know their schedules and deadlines will have a better understanding of how to work within those parameters and develop a priority list for their schoolwork. Students might benefit from a tutor. Encourage your children to find a tool (e.g. Google Calendar, a planner, or a checklist) that works for them and get in the habit of using that tool consistently. The important thing to remember is that we’re all in this together. None of us are the same as we were 18 months ago. But as we begin to make plans for the future, we can trust in our shared hope that our children can thrive once more. Emily Thompson is the Managing Director and Ariel Rodriguez is the Director of Operations at Study Smarter, LLC. It is a nonprofit organization that has presented summer musicals for over 50 years. Traditionally, three musicals are presented each summer. This year, after receiving clearance by Alameda County in early summer, two musicals are being presented, Hartog’s bedroom comedy The Fourposter serves as the basis for I Do! I Do!, a two-character musical. Originally directed by Gower Champion on Broadway, and with music by Harvey Schmidt, it features an evening-long journey through 50 years of marital bliss, infidelity, children, incompatibility, old age and simple joys. articles.text: H e l g i To m a s s o n h a s announced that he will retire as Artistic Director and Principal Choreographer of San Francisco Ballet by mid-2022. He has led the ballet company for nearly 40 years. “The unprecedented challenges we faced as individuals and as a community during 2020 only served to reconfirm for me the power of dance as a form of artistic expression, connection, and humanity. Over the past ten months, we had to innovate and completely reconceive how to bring dance to our audiences, since they could not come to us. In looking to the 2022 season, my aim is to build on these achievements and to bring the Company back to the stage for live performances,” Tomasson said. “Despite or perhaps because of the year we all lived through together, the Company has never been stronger than it is today. The timing felt right to begin a transition to a new Artistic Director, who will build on this legacy and lead the Company into its next chapter.” Tomasson was a distinguished dancer before assuming artistic leadership of San Francisco Ballet in 1985. articles.text: Legion of Honor, part of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, is exhibiting “Iliazd: Publishing as an Art Form” now through October. The exhibit draws from the collection of Ilia Zdanevich’s work in the Reva, and David Logan Collection of Illustrated Books, “Iliazd: Publishing as an Art Form” will look at the work of the Russian Modernist whose collaborators included Pablo Picasso, Georges Braque, Alberto Giacometti, Max Ernst, and Joan Miró. Zdanevich created and published twenty-one artists’ books while working in Paris from 1921 to 1975, sixteen of which currently are in the Fine Arts Museums’ collection. This is the first U.S. museum collection devoted to the work of Zdanevich in more than three decades. While the artist was not a publisher in the conventional sense, he could be described as a self-publishing book artist, who commissioned his more famous peers to produce images for his books. “An illustrated book by Iliazd is a book by Iliazd, and not a book by Picasso, Miró, or Max Ernst,” said Louis Barnier, Director of the Imprimerie Union, Paris. “[It is] a standalone work of art just like a painting, a sculpture, a monument, a film. And Iliazd is its true and sole creator.” The exhibition is included with general admission to the museum. Museum hours are Tuesdays through Sundays, 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. Visit https://legionof honor. famsf.org/exhibitions/iliazd to learn more and purchase tickets. Legion of Honor

articles.text: Winemaker Nicolas Potel with vineyard manager Sylvain Debord. Last month I wrote about the estate wines of Domaine de Bellene, the Burgundian winery run by Nicholas Potel. Because the estate, like most in Burgundy, is small with little wine to sell, Potel wanted to find a way to expose more people to the wines of Burgundy. That was the origin of Maison Roche de Bellene – his negociant firm. A wine negociant buys wine from outside producers and bottles it under its own label. The quality of negociants varies widely, as everything depends on the ability to find and secure good grapes. The son of a famous vintner, Nicholas grew up in Burgundy. During his teenage years he traveled up and down the Cote d’ Or on his bicycle trading wines with growers and establishing life-long friendships. He has been working with some of those growers ever since he started his first negociant company nearly 25 years ago in 1998. Nicholas arranges to buy wine from small producers who vintify the wine on their own property. Final assemblage and bottling of the wine is done at the Roche de Bellene winery in Savigny-les-Beaune. I found the portfolio to be chock full of excellent examples of their terroirs. I also found some to be excellent values considering the incredibly inflated prices Burgundians now charge for their wines. The Maison Roche de Bellene wines are imported by Loosen Bros. based in Salem, Oregon. www.loosenbrosusa.com This entry level Bourgogne is an excellent introduction to Burgundy.

articles.text: All of the different housing types we use can be divided into two main categories: single-family housing, and multi-family housing. While the vast majority of people in the industrialized urban world live in multi-family housing of one kind or another, in the U.S. an estimated 80% of housing units are single family, and 20-25% as multi family. There are a number of variations and hybrids, along with varying labels for the different types of housing but in my experience, the types shown in the accompanying diagram are common and understood by architects, developers, contractors and planners. For all communities the end result of different housing types is different densities, typically measured in units/acre. There is a huge difference from say, 3.5 units/acre for single family detached homes, to 12 units/acre for attached townhomes, to as many as 90 units/acre for urban high-rise multi-family. There are also many interconnected components to housing density and the resulting look, feel, and functioning of a neighborhood, including open space, roadway size and type, public transportation systems, and infrastructures of various kinds. (And parking, which we will leave for another column.) In my mind, a dividing line in the whole multi-family world can be defined by the entries. Units with their own separate outside entries, such as duplexes, townhouses or garden apartments, have a whole different character than denser types such as mid or high-rise buildings with entries necessarily located off a common corridor. The units in these denser, higher buildings can’t have the individuality, residential character and connection to the street that the lower density units do. The description of different architectural types of housing is sometimes confused with ownership categories. For example, a 10-unit “apartment” building can be owned by one person, in which case the 10 units would be rented out. This is the most common definition of “apartment”. But the same 10-unit building could also be a condominium, in which case the 10 occupants would each own the inside of their own unit with everything else being considered common space owned jointly by the 10 owners. In this case it would typically be called a “condo” and not an apartment building. Other forms of ownership such as co-ops are somewhat similar. In any case, these different types of ownership can be applied to all of the different architectural types, not just multi-family. Special purpose multi-family housing. like student housing, senior housing, affordable housing, or low-income housing, also can be designed in many of the architectural types, under a variety of ownership formulas, with the one-owner “apartment” model probably most common. Next: Multi-family Housing, Part 2 Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. Outside of central zones, like downtown Oakland or the Lake Merritt area, we are most familiar with single family detached (SFD) housing. Some “attached” single family units can be 4 times as dense as single-family dwellings, although still technically considered single family.

articles.text: Photos by Peter Chin Harry Lew’s Congressional Gold Medal award. Lake Park resident This year, much of Lake Park Retirement in Oakland proudly turned out to celebrate a fellow resident Harry Lew. We had learned that Harry was to receive a special rendition of the Congressional Gold Medal, recently authorized by Congress after a long campaign to honor the thousands of Chinese American GI’s who served in World War II. We later learned that Harry was part of the campaign to gain that recognition. Because of the Chinese Exclusion Act, Chinese immigrants and their American-born families remained ineligible for citizenship until 1943 during the war. The Certificate and Legion medal were conferred by Helen Wong, Commander of American Legion Cathay Post 384. articles.text: It’s OK to change your mind about being a caregiver. Often people take on caring for a family member with the best of intentions, but not knowing how long it will last, or how care needs will change, or how their own lives may evolve. They may find themselves ready for a new chapter or completely overwhelmed; some people even end up needing care for themselves after injury or illness resulting from overexertion as a caregiver. Consider these steps to change your caregiving role and maintain your own well-being: 1. Communicate, communicate, communicate. Talk to the health care provider and care team (maybe a professional caregiver, a physical or occupational therapist, etc.) about the status of current needs and anticipated care expectations for a loved one. Then plan a meeting with them and your loved one, or just share what you learned along with what you are capable of doing. Involve this person in the decisions as much as possible and share your limitations. 2. Do research together on interviewing caregivers, visiting facilities, reviewing insurance policies, and methods of paying for different long-term care options. In this way, the decisions are made together, and everyone is a stakeholder. If your loved one has a professional caregiver, and you are looking at a transition to a facility, it’s likely the caregiver can remain part of the care team for additional one-on-one care. 3. Take baby steps. If you’ve been doing all of the caregiving – driving Mom to and from medical appointments, making meals, giving medication reminders, assisting with bathing, being a companion to play games and socialize, and more – look into hiring a caregiver who can relieve you of a portion of these tasks so you can enjoy being a son, daughter, niece or nephew, grandchild, or spouse again. This way it does not have to be a big move, and you can oversee this new relationship and even be part of it. Remember that caregiving is a journey, not a destination, and will change over time for all involved. Feelings of guilt are normal and can be dealt with so that better choices can be made, helping avoid resentment and exhaustion, while continuing to be a caregiver. articles.text: A self-guided walking tour of Piedmont which follows the city’s eight and a half-mile perimeter has been created by resident Matt Gerhardt, who presented a map to the Park Commission at their August 4 meeting. The Recreation Commission will discuss how it plans to use this map at its meeting this evening, August 18, at 7:30 p.m. The idea was born of Gerhardt’s experience on one of the “Walking on Wednesdays” excursions. “After I joined [Walking on Wednesdays], I started going farther and farther, north and south, and was getting fairly far. One day, Marilyn Weber and I decided to just walk around the entire perimeter,” Gerhardt said. The route took about 3-1/2 hours, he said. “It’s definitely a ‘hike,’” Gerhardt said with a smile. “And it’s up and down hills – but it’s fun.” Weber told Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap about the idea, who asked the pair to share their route with Park commissioners. The next time Weber and Gerhardt took the route, Gerhardt geo-tagged it through Google maps, creating a digital ‘hike.’ “It could be fun to have a joint program with the Recreation Commission, to include his route,” Dunlap told commissioners. Walking on Wednesdays was created by Recreation Commissioner Dick Carter, who was excited to learn about Gerhardt’s initiative. “We have walked some aspects of the perimeter. I think it’s terrific and I commend Matt for creating the perimeter route,” Carter said. Carter added that the Walking on Wednesdays group has helped foster old and new relationships among community members. Several members have even splintered off into a reading group. He believes Gerhardt’s idea of a self-guided map will generate the same level of interest and community. The Recreation Commission will receive an update on the map tonight, and Park Commissioners stated their plans to work jointly to present Gerhardt’s map formally to the community. “I know many residents who walk, and it’s great to actually have a destination, rather than just walking,” Park Commissioner Betsy Goodman said. “This will be fun – whether you do part of it or all of it, I think people will really get a kick out of it.”

articles.text: Wednesday Walkers gather at the upper end of the Oakland Avenue Bridge on August 11. Pictured are: Phil Witte (left), Albert Chen, Elangovan Shanmuga Sundaram, Ken Young, Quincy Dong, Alicia Rivera, Noemi Alvarado, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Harriette Louie, Charlene Louie, Carol Lyons, Wenny Young, Susan Martin, Melba Yee, Jim Kuo, Sarah Johnson, Priscilla Wanerus, Nancy Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Nancy Olsen, Helen Dong, Susan Field, Swee Ling Chen, Mike Henn, Stella Houston, and Haybert Houston. There was another strong turnout for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays on August 11, with 28 walkers. Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen was there to tell the walkers about her new “Meet Ups” initiative. She encouraged the walkers to email their ideas to her at ephalen@piedmont.ca.gov. One park not recently visited was the Linda Avenue Dog Park, so the decision was made to visit it and the adjacent Oakland Avenue Bridge, the historic entrance to Piedmont. Drawing on Piedmont Historical Society information from Gail Lombardi’s research, the walkers learned that Albert Farr designed the bridge in 1910 as a significant entrance to Piedmont, then in its third year as an incorporated city. Farr used the same Spanish design that he had used in the Piedmont City Hall and the Bonita Avenue School, later named Havens School. The bridge replaced a wooden trestle built in 1890 for the cable cars that served Piedmont in its early years. The bridge was built in 1911 by Engineer John Buck Leonard of Union City, Michigan, who was a pioneering bridge engineer, architect, and an early advocate of reinforced concrete. The bridge has architectural motifs such as steep walls and overhangs which were once used to prevent entry into medieval fortresses. The concrete arch bridge over Linda Avenue has a 160-foot arch span and retaining wall supported approaches in a closed spandrel concrete deck arch design. The bridge’s total length is 343 feet. The bridge carried 7,675 cars in 2007, an average of 20 vehicles a day. The relatively new lampposts, lights, and now the guardrails make the Oakland Avenue Bridge a lovely entrance to the city. Many walkers had never been to the Linda Avenue Dog Park next to the bridge. As the group walked through the park, they were surprised how attractive it is and were impressed with the improvements the City has made. The group emerged on to Linda Avenue and passed the new townhomes that were built on a former PG&E substation near the base of the bridge. The walkers continued on to the corner of Linda and Grand Avenue. Regular walkers identified this as the site where Axel R. Gruggel built his A Mon Chateau restaurant and beer garden in 1892. The walkers lamented that the beer is long gone. They went down Grand, carefully crossed it at Ace Hardware, and made their climb back up Wildwood and Magnolia Avenues to the Exedra starting point. It had been a 90 minute, little over two mile walk with and new and old friends, and fun for everyone. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

Its large pool and hot tub are closed for repairs. From High Camp, walking to Squaw Peak is a two-mile straight shot and around 850 feet in elevation gain, with the final 0.6 mile to the peak as the greatest ascent. The trail averages less than 10 percent gradient for the first mile before making the climb to Squaw Peak. At the 1.3-mile mark, hikers will come to a junction with a path on the left going up toward the Siberia Express ski lift. The preferred trail on the right takes you along the back toward Squaw Peak. Squaw Valley staff advised The Post to take the trail on the right as opposed to the steep jaunt toward the ski lift on the left where park attendants are working. The trail provides an unforgettable walk with bushels of wildflowers lining the path and butterflies fluttering around, On the right is the magnificent Granite Chief Mountain and Desolation Wilderness. From Squaw Peak hikers get a clear view of Lake Tahoe and a glimpse of Five Lakes. Pack a lunch to eat while enjoying the view. There are also mounds of shale enclosures to protect from the wind if needed. Returning to High Camp from Squaw Peak will round out your day at four miles. Those interested can follow a trail on the left to the Gold Coast Express ski lift, and then up to the Watson Monument Emigrant Pass Marker. Walking to the marker adds .4 miles to your day and another 300 feet in elevation gain. The nearby peak to the left of the marker (when facing the plaque) gives an even closer look of Granite Chief. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew spent a weekend at the Enchanted Hills Camp for the Blind in Napa on August 14-15 to make repairs at the camp, maintain trails, and reduce fire fuel by clearing out dead branches. Approximately 20 crew members and adult advisors volunteered their time for the overnight adventure. The main project was building steps and handrails along steep sections of the camp trails to guide visually impaired campers. Although crew members have been volunteering at Enchanted Hills for several years, it was the first time they stayed overnight. “For many of the blind children who attend the camp every summer, this is one of their few opportunities to connect with others and feel a sense of support,” explained PCSC co-president Julia Banuelos. “We were able to get a glimpse of this impact through meeting one of the former campers. Impacted by fires in the area, the camp is undergoing a lot of work, especially by volunteers.” The crew worked to create steps by digging close fitting trenches to partially bury timbers across the steep slopes, then back filled behind the timbers with gravel. All the wood used was custom milled from damaged trees on the property. In two days, the crew installed 15 stairs and cleared a quarter mile of debris. After each long day of work, the crew took time to refuel with sausages, salads and soups made by crew members and volunteer parents. Since the temperature was nearly 90 degrees, everyone got to have a dip in the camp’s pool to cool off. “The work the other volunteers and I did was very rewarding, and the property was so beautiful,” explained 11th grader Sofia Prieto Black. “It gave me the opportunity to disconnect from the ‘real world’ and enabled me to fully enjoy the company, the delicious food, and the peaceful nature that surrounded us.” The group will plan a service day or overnight later this fall. “The entire experience was so much fun. pages.text: Wednesday, August 18, 2021 31 By Ava Adarkar The Piedmont Community Service Crew spent a weekend at the Enchanted Hills Camp for the Blind in Napa on August 14-15 to make repairs at the camp, maintain trails, and reduce fire fuel by clearing out dead branches. Approximately 20 crew members and adult advisors volunteered their time for the overnight adventure. The main project was building steps and handrails along steep sections of the camp trails to guide visually impaired campers. Although crew members have been volunteering at Enchanted Hills for several years, it was the first time they stayed overnight. “For many of the blind children who attend the camp every summer, this is one of their few opportunities to connect with others and feel a sense of support,” explained PCSC co-president Julia Banuelos. “We were able to get a glimpse of this impact through meeting one of the former campers.
